name: WW2 Pidgin German
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: Die KZ-typische Dominanz der deutschen Sprache prägte natürlich auch die Lagerszpracha, wobei diese das Deutsche auf spezifische Art veränderte: slavische Prä- und Suffixe bei Verben, Akzentwechsel, Nasalierungen, Genusendungen, Pluralbildungen etc.
new_statements.translation: The camp-typical dominance of the German language naturally also shaped the Lagerszpracha, which however altered German in specific ways: Slavic prefixes and suffixes on verbs, accent shifts, nasalizations, gender endings, plural formations, etc.
new_statements.citation: Oschlies, Wolf. 2004. Sprache in nationalsozialistischen Konzentrationslagern. Theorie und Empirie der 'Lagerszpracha'. Online essay, Zukunft braucht Erinnerung (6 Nov 2004), condensing Oschlies 1985 (zeitgeschichte 13(1): 1-27) and 1986 (Muttersprache 96: 98-109).
new_statements.locator: section on the lexical/morphological peculiarities of the Lagerszpracha (unpaginated web essay; paragraph beginning 'Die KZ-typische Dominanz der deutschen Sprache')
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: the sentence "Die KZ-typische Dominanz der deutschen Sprache prägte natürlich auch die Lagerszpracha, wobei diese das Deutsche auf spezifische Art veränderte: slavische Prä- und Suffixe bei Verben, Akzentwechsel, Nasalierungen, Genusendungen, Pluralbildungen etc." is present character-for-character in (offset 13926), in the closing paragraph of Oschlies's 2004 ZbE essay, immediately after the 'extra prima Saloniki' passage and before the 'political culture' proposal. It is the only occurrence of Akzent/Beton*/Silbe/Aussprache in the essay (one other hit: 'Lexik, Phonetik, Anwendung etc.' at offset 5040, a bare list). No placement, no example, no secondary stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given anywhere. The only stress-related remark in any accessible source is that the camp pidgin changed the accent of the German words it took over ('Akzentwechsel'), presumably toward the Slavic speakers' patterns; the two primary descriptions (Max 1946, Unbegaun 1947) are wordlist-level and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Refers to German lexical items as re-shaped in prisoners' speech; no word/phrase distinction, no examples with marked stress. Max 1946 (p.173) notes only pronunciations such as nicht -> 'nix' and Schonung -> 'schono' (p.170); Unbegaun 1947 characterizes the sabir as German-based, nouns in bare nominative without article, verbs in the infinitive.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog ww2p1234 is the German-based inter-ethnic pidgin ('sabir international', Unbegaun; 'sabir', Max; Oschlies's 'Lagerszpracha') of the WWII concentration camps (observations mainly Buchenwald 1944 and Dachau); Glottolog's two references are the only primary descriptions. The Polish-based Auschwitz 'lagerszpracha'/'krematoryjne esperanto' described by Wesołowska, Jagoda et al. and Leżak is a related but Polish-matrix variety; Straka 1946 describes the Czech national argot of Buchenwald, not the pidgin.
